title: Discrimination of genuinely nonlocal sets without entanglement in multipartite systems
authors: Ziying Hou, Huaqi Zhou, Limin Gao
abstract: Genuine nonlocality arises when a set of multipartite orthogonal states is locally indistinguishable under any bipartition of the subsystems. The entanglement-assisted discrimination of such genuinely nonlocal orthogonal product sets has attracted significant attention in quantum information. Based on the criterion of local irreducibility, genuine nonlocality is classified into Type I (reducible) and Type II (irreducible). We present entanglement-assisted discrimination schemes for both types of genuinely nonlocal sets that use minimal resources. For low-dimensional cases, Type I sets require only a single EPR pair, whereas Type II sets necessitate only one GHZ state. We extend these protocols to higher-dimensional systems: the discrimination of Type I sets requires only one maximally entangled state in a two-qutrit system, while that of Type II sets similarly demands a single maximally entangled state in a three-qutrit system. For $n$-partite ($n > 3$) systems, Type I sets continue to require only one maximally entangled state, whereas Type II sets necessitate just one additional EPR pair compared to their Type I counterparts. These results provide a robust framework for the efficient discrimination of genuinely nonlocal sets using minimal quantum resources.
summary: This paper develops comprehensive protocols to distinguish between genuinely nonlocal sets of orthogonal product states in multipartite quantum systems. By classifying these sets into Type I and Type II based on local reducibility, the authors determine the minimal entanglement resources required for perfect discrimination. The results provide a general framework applicable from bipartite up to $n$-partite systems.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of perfectly discriminating between sets of quantum states that exhibit genuine nonlocality in multipartite systems.
main_result: It establishes robust, resource-efficient protocols showing that discrimination requires minimal entanglement resources, such as a single EPR pair or GHZ state, depending on the type and dimensionality of the nonlocal set.
method: The core method involves constructing multi-step measurement sequences using local operations and classical communication (LOCC), supplemented by shared ancillary entangled states to overcome inherent nonlocality barriers.
model_or_system: The system consists of multipartite orthogonal product quantum states defined over tensor products of qudit spaces ($\mathbb{C}^{d_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes \mathbb{C}^{d_n}$). The sets are classified as Type I (reducible) or Type II (irreducible) based on local indistinguishability.
key_observables: The outcomes of sequential local projective measurements ($M_k$) performed by different subsystems (Alice, Bob, Charlie) serve as the primary diagnostics for state identification.
important_parameters: The required entanglement resources are key parameters, including single EPR pairs ($\vert\phi^+(2)angle$), GHZ states ($\vert G(3)angle$), and maximally entangled states in higher-dimensional systems.
main_assumptions: The protocols assume the existence of specific maximally entangled resource states and that the sets being discriminated are indeed genuinely nonlocal but locally distinguishable given sufficient entanglement assistance.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first defining genuine nonlocality, then presenting specialized discrimination schemes for low-dimensional bipartite systems (Type I/II), generalizing these protocols to tripartite and $n$-partite systems using increasing levels of shared entanglement resources.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous theoretical framework for quantifying the minimum quantum resources needed to verify fundamental properties like genuine nonlocality, which is crucial for quantum cryptography and foundational tests of quantum mechanics.
